facts.fact_text: On 6 March 2005 the applicant took part in a demonstration to mark the Women's Day celebrations in Beyazıt Square in Istanbul.
On 6 March 2005 people began gathering at different locations in order to march towards Beyazıt Square.
At around 11.30 a.m. on 6 March 2005 the dispersed groups gathered in Beyazıt Square and read out a press statement.
During the demonstration on 6 March 2005 in Beyazıt Square, police officers did not prevent people from entering the square.
During the demonstration on 6 March 2005 in Beyazıt Square, police officers did not interfere with the demonstrations.

When the crowds began to disperse after the Women's Day celebrations on 6 March 2005, police officers started hitting people, including the applicant, with their truncheons and the ends of their weapons.
When the crowds began to disperse after the Women's Day celebrations on 6 March 2005, police officers sprayed people, including the applicant, with tear gas.
As a result of blows to her head, face and other parts of her body, the applicant fell to the ground during the incident on 6 March 2005.
Whilst the applicant was on the ground, police officers continued to kick and hit her with their sticks.
Police officers swore at the applicant and insulted her during the incident on 6 March 2005.
The applicant was seriously injured during the incident on 6 March 2005.
The applicant was left semi-conscious as a result of the incident on 6 March 2005.
The applicant had to be helped by a member of the public to leave the area after the incident on 6 March 2005.
The video footage shows police officers wearing gas masks hitting with their truncheons a large number of demonstrators who try to run away from the area.
The video footage shows demonstrators who had fallen to the ground being kicked and hit with truncheons by police officers.
The video footage shows a male demonstrator who uses his body to protect a woman on the ground being kicked in the face by a police officer.
The video footage shows police officers spraying demonstrators hiding in bushes with tear gas before hitting them with their truncheons.
The video footage shows two women on the ground trying to protect themselves from attacks by police officers being sprayed with tear gas.
The video footage shows women who had taken refuge in nearby shops and cafes being dragged out by the police and beaten up.

According to the report prepared by the expert appointed by the domestic investigating authorities, police had hit the demonstrators — including those who had fallen to the ground — with their truncheons, kicked them, punched them and sprayed them with tear gas on 6 March 2005.

Section 10 of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law No. 2911) provides that in order for a meeting to take place, the governor's office or authorities of the district in which the demonstration is planned must be informed, during opening hours and at least seventy-two hours prior to the meeting, by a notice containing the signature of all the members of the organising board.

Section 22 of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law No. 2911) provides that demonstrations organised in public squares must comply with security instructions and not disrupt individuals' movement or public transport.

Section 24 of the Meetings and Demonstration Marches Act (Law No. 2911) provides that demonstrations and processions which do not comply with the provisions of the Act will be dispersed by force on the order of the governor's office and after the demonstrators have been warned.

The trial court found that some of the defendant police officers exceeded the limits of their powers on the use of force and used excessive force.

The trial court concluded that police officers M.C., A.O.P., S.B., Y.K. and E.B. had used excessive force against the demonstrators and committed the offence of ill-treatment defined in section 245 of the Criminal Code then in force (Law No. 765).

The trial court found police officer C.U. guilty of the offence of causing grievous bodily harm while using his powers as a public official, an offence defined in section 86 § 3 of the Criminal Code now in force (Law No. 5237), for having broken a bone of one of the demonstrators.
On 6 June 2005 the disciplinary board of the police considered that six police officers had kicked the demonstrators and had also hit them with their truncheons during the incident of 6 March 2005.
The disciplinary board of the police held that the six police officers' actions during the incident of 6 March 2005 amounted to 'degrading behaviour'.
The disciplinary board of the police decided to 'condemn' the actions of three police chiefs for failing to train the six police officers properly.

The disciplinary board of the police imposed a fine equivalent to three days' salary on the six police officers who had kicked the demonstrators and hit them with their truncheons during the incident of 6 March 2005.

The remaining forty-eight defendant police officers were acquitted by the trial court for lack of evidence.

According to information provided to the Court by the Government on 10 November 2011, the criminal proceedings against the police officers were discontinued on 8 September 2011 on account of the statute of limitations.
The applicant's objection against the Istanbul prosecutor's decision of 12 December 2005 was rejected on 28 September 2007 by the Beyoğlu Assize Court.
In the indictment filed on 9 December 2005, forty-nine persons, including the applicant, were listed as victims and complainants.
The trial court noted that the victims and complainants complained of having been injured when the defendant police officers kicked them, punched them and hit them with their truncheons and shields.
The trial court noted that the victims and complainants complained of having been excessively sprayed with tear gas by the defendant police officers.
The trial court noted that the victims and complainants stated that the defendant police officers had been wearing gas masks and hiding the identification numbers on their uniforms.

The trial court noted that the victims and complainants stated that the attacks had taken place very suddenly and when they had already been affected by tear gas, making it impossible to identify the police officers individually.
The trial court noted that the large numbers of defendants and victims, coupled with the fact that this was a large-scale incident, resulted in delays in obtaining all the evidence.
The trial court noted that the trial was also delayed as a result of the defendants' covering their faces with helmets and not displaying their identification numbers.

The trial court found, having examined the video footage of the events as well as the reports and witness statements, that it was not possible to expect the victims to identify the police officers who attacked them because it was not possible to recognise the police officers in the video footage.

The inspectors who had questioned the police officers were heard in the course of the trial proceedings and confirmed the authenticity and accuracy of the statements they had taken from the police officers.

The trial court found that the inspectors' statements were corroborated by the video footage which shows the punching, kicking, hitting with truncheons and shields, and using an excessive amount of tear gas.
